This is burnout, and if you want to survive as a trader, you must learn to recognize it.

True burnout is not just being overworked, nor is it something you can push through. It is a feedback loop that occurs when your body experiences intense, prolonged stress.

Stress is part of life, and under normal conditions you can recover from it easily. In fact, many dimensions of human performance - strength, endurance, mental acuity - actually require stress in order to grow.

However, growth in response to stress can only happen when the stress is manageable and offset by periods of recovery. When the stress is extreme and constant, the body fails to adapt and enters a downward spiral.

As stress accumulates, several things happen physiologically:
- sleep is disrupted
- hormones become dysregulated
- mental performance degrades
- heart rate variability falls 
- inflammation rises and immune function declines

The problem is that each of these effects also *reduces your ability to withstand and recover from stress.* So you enter a vicious cycle where recovery becomes impossible and performance steadily deteriorates.

The experience @agapestride describes here is exactly what it feels like to burn out from trading. And if you find yourself in this situation, the most important thing you can do is *recognize what has happened.* 

You are not dumber than you used to be. You are not more indecisive. You are not more impulsive, fearful, or greedy. You are simply physiologically impaired by severe, chronic stress.

When you notice the signs of burnout, you must prioritize recovery above all else:
- cut your risk
- stop looking at charts
- get off social media
- play sports or start running
- spend time with friends and family
- go hiking or traveling
- take lots of hot baths

As much as it feels like the best time to make generational wealth is RIGHT NOW, the market will always be here. So take a break and don't come back until you know your body can handle it.

Something I notice: adrenaline, dopamine, and fatigue stack up during a great win streak. It’s incredibly hard to stop trading, and as the fatigue builds, I’m tempted to size up tremendously. Part of me is relieved when the big loss finally hits, because it warrants a break.

The issue is that in most instances, like last week, if I had never sized up, I most likely wouldn’t have lost much, if anything. Smaller sizing preserves control. In that particular case, I was FORCED to close my positions so my remaining margin wouldn’t get wiped. Third, the technological risk. AI is advancing at an incredible pace, with companies like OpenAI pushing the boundaries of what's possible, while quantum computing continues to develop. Both could pose serious long-term challenges to the cryptographic security that much of the crypto market relies on. I don't think the market is adequately pricing in these risks, and I believe the gap between technological progress and market awareness could become a major headwind for crypto.

My thesis isn't simply "the market has topped."

It's that a strengthening dollar, bearish technicals, and the growing threat AI and quantum computing pose to crypto's underlying security could create the perfect storm for risk assets.

Could I be wrong? Absolutely. If the DXY thesis fails or the market reclaims key resistance levels, I'll reassess.

But right now, I believe the risk is heavily skewed to the downside, particularly for altcoins.

$BTC has been ranging between roughly $82,500 and $87,500 for quite some time now. That’s basically a $5K box, and we've spent a lot of time moving back and forth inside it.

My view is that we're still in a big liquidity-hunting phase.

Price moves towards the highs, takes liquidity and liquidates shorts, then reverses and moves towards the lows, where longs get liquidated. Then it happens again.

That’s one of the main reasons I think so many people are getting chopped up in this range.

And honestly, this is exactly where I don't want to overtrade.

A $5K range can look like there are endless opportunities, but if you keep chasing every move, using too much leverage or FOMOing into candles, the market can take your money on both sides before it eventually chooses a direction.

I'm not here to convince everyone that my scenario has to happen. It's simply how I currently see the market.

That’s why I told my X subscribers that, in my opinion, the higher-probability move was a rotation back towards the lower end of the range at $82,500.

And that’s exactly what happened this morning.

$82,500 was also TP1 of our accumulation strategy, so obviously it's always nice to see a level and target play out as expected.

But I think there’s something more important happening here.

My view is that we're still in a big liquidity-hunting phase.

Price moves towards the highs, takes liquidity and liquidates shorts, then reverses and moves towards the lows, where longs get liquidated. Then it happens again.

That’s one of the main reasons I think so many people are getting chopped up in this range.

And honestly, this is exactly where I don't want to overtrade.

A $5K range can look like there are endless opportunities, but if you keep chasing every move, using too much leverage or FOMOing into candles, the market can take your money on both sides before it eventually chooses a direction.

For me, the plan is pretty simple now.

I want to see how Bitcoin reacts around the range.

If we break below $82,500 and get confirmation, I think the downside can accelerate.

The range is roughly $5K wide, so a basic measured move would put us around $77,500. My broader target is still somewhere in the mid-$70Ks, which is also the view I shared publicly about a month ago.

A lot of people didn't believe me back then.

And that's completely fine.

I'm not here to convince everyone that my scenario has to happen. It's simply how I currently see the market.

It could be wrong. What matters to me is having a plan for both scenarios.

For now, I don't want to FOMO into big candles and I don't want to force trades in the middle of the range.

The month is still long.

I'll keep some % as dry powder and would rather have capital available if we get lower prices than deploy everything just because the market starts moving.

Patience is important in these conditions.

Let the market come to you. Don't chase it.
